nameStory: The 'spathulate' in this moonwort's name comes from 'spatula,' referring to the distinctive spoon-shaped segments of its fronds that look remarkably like tiny kitchen spatulas. Like other moonworts, it gets its magical name from old folklore that claimed these mysterious ferns were most potent when gathered by moonlight.
description: Spathulate moonwort is one of New England's rarest and most elusive ferns, standing just a few inches tall with a unique two-part structure. Each plant produces a single sterile frond with distinctive spoon-shaped leaflets and a separate fertile spike that bears the spores. This tiny fern is so uncommon that it's been spotted only three times in all of New England, making it a true botanical treasure for those lucky enough to encounter it.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Distinctive spoon-shaped (spatulate) leaflet segments that feel thick and fleshy to the touch, quite different from typical thin fern leaflets

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Tiny stature, typically just 2-4 inches tall, with a single sterile frond and separate fertile spike emerging from underground

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Short, fleshy stem that feels almost succulent-like rather than the typical wiry fern stipe texture

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spores produced on a separate branched spike (not on the leafy frond), with tiny round clusters that release golden dust when mature

habitat: This extremely rare moonwort favors undisturbed grassy areas, meadows, and forest openings with well-drained but not dry soils. It typically grows in calcareous (lime-rich) soils and seems to prefer areas with some disturbance history but not current trampling.

seasonality.spring: Fronds emerge directly from the ground without the typical fiddlehead stage, appearing as small, distinctive spoon-shaped leaves.
seasonality.summer: Prime viewing season when both sterile fronds and fertile spikes are fully developed and most easily spotted.
seasonality.fall: Spores are released and fronds begin to yellow and wither, becoming much harder to locate.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant underground with no visible above-ground parts remaining.

funFact: This moonwort is so rare and secretive that it can remain completely underground for years at a time, only popping up when conditions are just right—meaning a population could be hiding beneath your feet without any visible sign!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other tiny moonworts, but the distinctive spoon-shaped leaflet segments are unique—think of tiny spatulas rather than the more typical triangular or oval shapes of other moonworts.
contextualKnowledge: Moonworts belong to an ancient fern family that's quite different from typical ferns—they don't form fiddleheads and their spores are produced on separate structures rather than on the backs of leaves, representing a more primitive evolutionary stage.
compareHints: Unlike its moonwort relatives with their more typical triangular or oval leaflet shapes, spathulate moonwort's spatula-shaped segments are unmistakable. While little grapefern is similarly tiny, its leaflets are more rounded, and matricary grapefern has much more finely divided, lacy foliage rather than the simple spoon shapes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Matricary grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its chamomile-like leaf segments that are more finely divided than most of its relatives.
Narrow triangle moonwort differs from matricary grapefern by having much narrower, more pointed segments rather than finely dissected, lacy ones.
**[Uncertain claim flagged: specific comparison details]** Swamp moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for wet habitats and its small, fan-shaped sterile frond segments.
Little grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its simple, often undivided leaf blade, whereas matricary grapefern and others have multiple leaflets or more complex divisions.

Upswept moonwort differs from other moonworts by its fan or wedge-shaped leaflet segments that angle upward, rather than the more rounded or deeply divided segments of relatives like matricary grapefern.
Prairie moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for dry, prairie-like conditions rather than the moist, shaded habitats preferred by most of its relatives.
